narrow_notes.N1: The most burdened group in the set: 19.6% of income before any credit, ahead of every other archetype. Older owners living alone, long settled. Almost all are PTFC-eligible, the median one already draws the senior maximum, and they are STILL above the 6% line after claiming it. The credit is working and the burden remains. 86% sit at the cap, so they gain only if the maximum rises; the benefit base does almost nothing for them.
narrow_notes.N2: The same age profile as N1 on 2.4x the income ($61,892 against $25,838), and a burden 7.7 points lighter. 55% sit at the cap, against 86% in N1, so the benefit base does as much work here as the maximum credit. The contrast with N1 is the clearest evidence in the set that what drives burden among older owners is living alone rather than age.
narrow_notes.N3: Working-age owner living alone. Too young for the senior benefit base or the senior cap, and no dependent uplift. Lower income than N4 on a markedly cheaper house, which is why its burden is worse. Age, not wealth, is what separates it from N1.
narrow_notes.N4: Working-age owner living with a partner, no dependents. Among the higher-income owner archetypes, so fewer of them qualify, and the mildest burden of the owner set. Present because the burdened group is not only the old and the poor. Base-bound rather than cap-bound: 42% at the cap against 58% for N5, which is why the two are kept apart despite similar burdens.
narrow_notes.N5: Owner with children or other dependents at home. The newest to their homes of any owner archetype: the median moved in 5-9 years ago and 36% within the last four years. The dependent test runs BEFORE the value test, so a family with children in a $2,000,000 house is N5 rather than N6. Its dependents lift the benefit base, which is why its post-credit burden lands below N1's despite a much larger bill.
narrow_notes.N6: Owner of a high-value home. The largest bills of any archetype and the smallest share eligible, because income disqualifies about half. The only archetype whose burden barely moves after the credit, 11.8% to 10.8%: the cap binds long before the bill does. Both the case for a liability ceiling and the case against it.
narrow_notes.N7: All burdened renters. The youngest, poorest and most recently moved of any group here, nearly all eligible (93%), and the credit does more work here than anywhere else, cutting the burden roughly in half. TWO CAUTIONS. A renter's 'tax' is the statutory 15% of rent, a proxy rather than a bill anyone receives. And 63% of this group reports annual rent exceeding annual income, which is not a sustainable budget and means cash income understates their resources; the 16.7% burden is indicative rather than comparable with an owner's.
